transcript: on my final day at the Edinburgh Fringe I saw The Gummy Bears’ Great War A Letter to Lyndon B Johnson or God, Whoever Reads This First The Gummy Bears Great War is a theater piece from Italy about a population of gummy bears that declares war against a population of dinosaurs it kinda uses the format of micro puppetry with as you can see real gummy bears laid out on a table in front of an intimate audience but it does mix in some traditional human acting as well The format is incredibly inventive and I think really embodies the spirit of fringe the show strikes a very distinct tone where there's obviously a certain element of absurdity and silliness but also a genuinely tragic undercurrent to this story about gummy bears trying to liberate themselves from the threat of being eaten despite no hope of success that blend of the ridiculous and the maudlin left me a little bit unsure what to make of the show as I was watching it but left a lot to chew on afterward (no pun intended) A Letter to Lyndon B Johnson or God Whoever Reads This First this is a play written and performed by the duo Xhloe and Natasha it's about two Boy Scouts in the 1960s who are obsessed with living up to a traditionally masculine and patriotic ideal the show is quite fun in a lot of ways there's a really infectious quality to the way they play these young boys the play also incorporates a lot of movement work in the vein of clown tradition but it also has a distinct style of its own that kind of embraces the corniness of youth and boyhood but also the corniness of the 1960s I know this sounds silly but the description that keeps coming to my mind is that the movement reminded me of like cartoon frogs so it can be very fun and funny but there's also a darker tragedy looming over the play as it alludes to the pipeline from Boy Scouts to military life the play was told largely through narration which as I always say is a bit of an obstacle for me and I do think I might have connected to the piece a bit more if it had been traditionally dramatized but there was definitely enough there dramatically, thematically, and visually to draw me in
